newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed accused of plot, denies charges.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed accused of plot, denies charges.

text.p: Russia's interior minister ordered security to be tightened across the country on Wednesday after accusing security chief Alexander Lebed of plotting to seize power while President Boris Yeltsin awaits heart surgery.
But Lebed dismissed Kulikov's accusations and added that he was fairly confident the president would back him.
General Anatoly Kulikov said tougher precautions were needed because of intelligence reports about planned attacks by rebels from breakaway Chechnya, but gave no details of the measures.
Kulikov, Lebed's bitter political foe, had said earlier on Wednesday that Yeltsin's security supremo was planning a "creeping coup" with the aid of Chechen rebels.
"There cannot even be talk of an attempted coup d'etat," Lebed told a hastily-called news conference. "Nothing will happen...unless Kulikov stirs things up."

"(Lebed) has decided to move ahead using force instead of waiting for the next presidential poll," Kulikov told an earlier news conference. "The question is what awaits Russia if Lebed comes to power through a creeping coup."
Lebed said he would press charges against Kulikov and said he was sure his rival would be fired over the incident.
"I am not sure that I'll be the one to be fired. It will be Kulikov who is fired," said Lebed, who in August told Yeltsin he would have to choose between one of the two men.
Yeltsin, whose surgery doctors have set for mid-November, expressed concern at Kulikov's charges and demanded details. "I bet seven-to-three that he will back me," Lebed said.
Kulikov later said on television he had agreed on the need for tougher security with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Moscow police could not immediately confirm that any special measures had been taken. "We have received no specific orders so far," a senior police officer said late on Wednesday.
There was no extra police on Moscow streets by midnight.

Chernomyrdin summoned Kulikov, Kovalyev, Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and other security officials to a meeting on Thursday which Itar-Tass news agency said would discuss the row between Lebed and Kulikov.
A Yeltsin spokesman told Interfax news agency that the president had demanded a report on Kulikov's accusations from Chernomyrdin and the interior minister himself.

The row marked a further heightening of a power struggle which has intensified since Yeltsin announced on September 5 that he would need a heart operation. Yeltsin appealed for an end to the "verbal duels" on Tuesday.
Sergei Mironov, head of the Kremlin medical centre, made clear on Wednesday that Yeltsin had had a blood problem but it had now cleared up and his operation would not be delayed.
Yeltsin met President Alexander Lukashenko of Belarus at the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow. He moved slowly and his eyes were puffy in brief television footage.
Yeltsin dropped out of public view shortly before he was reelected on July 3. He had two heart attacks last year and one surgeon says he may have had a third this summer.
He has handed some of his duties to Chernomyrdin, but many officials have been jostling for position.

Lebed, 46, has not hidden his presidential ambitions since Yeltsin made him secretary of his influential Security Council last June after he came third in the presidential election. He has many rivals in the Kremlin.
Kulikov is a bitter opponent of a peace deal which Lebed had signed with separatist rebels to end 21 months of war in the sourthern region. He says the deal humiliated Russia.
Lebed said on Wednesday that Lebed planned to set up an elite "legion" to stage a mutiny and that he had been promised 1,500 Chechen gunmen to help.
Interfax quoted the rebels as denying the charge and Lebed said all plans for a new mobile force had been discussed with Kulikov and others. He dismissed the idea of Chechen involvment.

The drama overshadowed a visit to Moscow by U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, intended to persuade parliament to ratify the START-2 treaty which would slash the number of strategic nuclear warheads to a third of Cold War levels.
Rodionov said after talks with Perry that he hoped parliament would ratify the treaty.
